Lock Queue

Reads a PostgreSQL migration and works out what it does to a table that is being used. The outage nobody plans for is not a slow migration — it is the queue. Your ALTER waits for the query already running, and every query that arrives after it waits behind the ALTER, including plain SELECTs. A 200ms migration stuck behind one slow report blocks the table for as long as that report runs.

What each statement does

Every statement that touches an existing table, the lock it takes, and how long it holds it at the row count above. Where there is a safer way to get the same result, the rewrite is given in full.

    Problems with the script as a whole

    Faults that come from how the statements are arranged rather than from any one of them.

      Estimates, not predictions. Durations come from the row count at roughly 500k rows/sec for a rewrite, 2M for a scan and 1M for an index build. Row width, disk and cache move these a lot. Use them to tell "instant" from "minutes", not to plan a maintenance window to the second.

      Pattern-based, not a parser. It recognises the shapes migrations actually take. Anything it does not recognise is listed and left unjudged rather than guessed at.

      Postgres 11 and later assumed. Adding a column with a constant default is catalog-only from 11, and SET NOT NULL can lean on a validated CHECK from 12.
